item.title: Single vs Multi Lane Waiting
item.description:
Introduction

Whenever you step into a bank or a grocery store, you encounter one of two queueing designs:

  1. Multi-Line Queuing ($c \times M/M/1$): Each register or counter has its own dedicated line. Customers pick a line and wait.
  2. Single-Line Queuing ($M/M/c$): A single “serpentine” line feeds into all available counters. The person at the front goes to the next open station.

While multi-line setups might feel faster because individual lines look shorter, single-line systems are mathematically superior in both average wait time and queue stability. Using Markov Chain theory and Queueing Theory, we can prove why pooling capacity eliminates systemic inefficiencies.

item.title: Deploy local AI via Ollama, Open-WebUI and VSCode/VSCodium
item.description:
This guide walks you through installing Ollama on a Linux system, serving it to a strictly local localhost WebUI (ensuring no exposure to the internet), and leveraging your local Large Language Models (LLMs) as an AI Chat Agent and autocomplete engine inside VSCode and/or VSCodium.

Why this setup is super cool?

  • No root / sudo required: Everything runs cleanly within your user space.
  • 100% Private: No reverse proxies or exposed external ports—just a local Python environment and standard tools.
  • Offline & Data Friendly No data tracking by Big Tech. (Yet you can configure the models in Open-WebUI to search the internet with e.g. DuckDuckGo (DDGS) if you want to.)
  • Completely Free No accounts, API keys, or monthly subscriptions. Only the electricity bill.

However…

  • GPU Requirements: Ollama is only fun, when you have a potent GPU. It also runs on my Laptop with a decent CPU and built-in Intel GPU, but you have to stick to small (=dumpish) models for fast responses. So, if you have a GPU, then let’s go!
  • AI Server: If you want to build your own AI server that is available from anywhere (e.g. you can access it from your phone), then you need to expose the Ollama server to the internet, preferralbly via a reverse proxy such as Caddy, Apache or Nginx. This is not covered in this guide.
  • This guide is for Linux but Windows and MacOS should works as well. Yet, I haven’t tested it.

item.title: Avoid Python Package Import-Errors in VSCodium or VSCode
item.description:
If you are working with Conda environments, you might notice that VSCodium or VS Code shows “import not found” errors (red squiggly lines) even though your code runs perfectly fine in the terminal.

This happens because the IDE’s Python extension doesn’t automatically know which Conda environment to use for its background linting and IntelliSense. By explicitly setting the interpreter path, you tell the IDE exactly where to look for your installed packages.

item.title: Use Neoylayout
item.description:
This is a short summary of the essentials of the keybord layout neo-layout variant bone for faster and healtier text (and math) typing on your PC.

Windows

To use it on Windows follow these steps.

Install

  • Copy the kbdbone.dll file in System32 to C:\Windows\System32 and the one in SysWOW64 to C:\Windows\SysWOW64 respectively. Grant access rights. (On 64-bit Windows you have to copy it with a 64-bit Programm, best by the Windows Explorer)

  • Execute the kbdneo_win10_install.reg file, which will add the layout to the registry for you. Again, grant access.

  • Reboot your system

  • In System Settings under Time&Language/Language choose the System Language and choose Bone as your keyboard layout.

  • At each boot: execute reneo.exe (e.g. via Tasksheduler)

item.title: Conda
item.description:
Why Conda?

Conda is an environment and package management system, widely used in scientific computing and data science. Very handy if you program in Python. Conda features:

  • Cross-Platform Compatibility
  • Package Management
  • Environment Management (you can switch easily)
  • Version control
  • Dependency Management

The handy thing about conda is that you can create a new environment for each project that you have. Then you install all the packages for each project in it’s own dedicated environment. Then you can swap back and forth to another project that might need totally different packages and versions. The different packages and versions are kind of ‘containerized’ and don’t interfer with each other.

item.title: Git Delete Commit History
item.description:
There are actually two possible methods, I recommend method 1.

Method 1

Create a new temporary orphan branch, delete the main branch and rename the temporary branch to main.

git pull origin main # Make sure your on the last version
git checkout --orphan temporary_branch # Create new branch
git add -A # Add all current content to
git commit -am "Initial commit" # Commit all content to temporary_branch
git branch -D main # Remove main branch
git branch -m main # Rename current temporary_branch to main
git push -f origin main # Force push to main
git remote prune origin # Prune old associations

All done!

item.title: How to include Scalable Vector Graphics (svg) in $\LaTeX$
item.description:
You may know the popular LaTeX package graphicx which you can use as:

\includegraphics[options]{filename}

graphicx does not support svg, but there is the package called svg that does the job.

How to use the svg package:

  1. Install Inkscape

    On Windows you can use winget.

    winget install -e --id Inkscape.Inkscape

  2. Copy your image.svg file into your document root folder (= right next to your .tex file)

  3. This is a MWE for your .tex file:

    \documentclass{article}
\includepackage{svg}
\begin{document}
 \begin{figure}
 \includesvg[]{image}
 \end{figure}
\end{document}

item.title: How to solve git VPN issue
item.description:
If you try to use git you can get the following error:

fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/yourusername/yourrepository.git/': Could not resolve host: github.com

This error can happen, if you are using a VPN.

The solution is to either toggle your VPN and try again or (if you don’t want to toggle your VPN) to execute:

  • If your VPN is currently OFF:

    git config --global --unset http.proxy

  • If your VPN is currently ON:

    git config --global --set http.proxy

item.title: Linear Regression
item.description:
Overview

Why and when do we need linear regression? In a nutshell, linear regression is used to predict data that has a linear relationship. That means all the datapoints are roughly on a straight line (in 2D), resp. on a hyperplane (in 3D). Firstly, we find some expression for the linear relationship (e.g. in 2D: $y=a\cdot x + b$; where $a$ is the slope and $b$ is the y-intercept). Secondly, we use this expression to insert some data where we only know the $x$ value, but want to predict their unknown $y$ value.

item.title: OpenPGP
item.description:
Hello,

You do not know what OpenPGP is? Then read the text below.

🔐 OpenPGP Public Key Verification
OpenPGP Cryptographic Key
UID / Identity: JF
Expires: Never
ASCII Armored Public Key
💾 Download Key (.asc)

What is OpenPGP?

Unfortunately, our emails are currently not encrypted by default. It is therefore very likely that government agencies (NSA and co.) and hackers can read our emails. This is not a desirable state of affairs. Encrypting email content with OpenPGP (PGP stands for ‘Pretty Good Privacy’) provides a remedy. A public key, with which the message is encrypted, and a private (secret) key, with which the message can be decrypted, are generated. As the name suggests, the public key can be made accessible to everyone, because how else can others write to you in encrypted form? The private key, on the other hand, must be kept safe so that it does not fall into the wrong hands.

item.title: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus
item.description:
Introduction

In our previous article, Backpropagation in Standard Calculus, we derived the gradient update equations using scalar notation. While standard calculus builds an intuitive understanding of how error flows through individual connections, writing code using scalar loops is computationally inefficient.

In practice, modern machine learning libraries (like PyTorch or TensorFlow) compute updates over entire layers simultaneously using Matrix Calculus and linear algebra routines optimized for GPUs.

This article formalizes backpropagation in vector and matrix notation.

item.title: Feedforward Phase
item.description:
Introduction

This article gives a quick overview over the feedforward phase of a Neural Network.

Nodes

A Neural Network is made of many Nodes that are connected to each other. Each Node itself is a very basic unit that does only do three things.

  1. Multiply each input with a weight and sum all inputs up. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i$, where $m$ is the number of inputs.
  2. Process the single, scalar input value by some activation function $y_{out}=f(y_{in})$ where $y_{in}$ is the result from step 1 and $y_{out}$ is the result from step 1 after being applied to the activation function.
  3. Output the result $y_{out}$ to the next node

item.title: Backpropagation in Standard Calculus
item.description:
Introduction

This article explains backpropagation of a Neural Network using standard scalar calculus notation. If you want to know how backpropagation is done using vectors and matrices, read this article: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus

Learning Process

Consider a 2-layer Neural Network (one hidden layer and one output layer) as shown below. We want to train the network so that the training inputs $x$ correctly produce the expected target labels $t$.

For training, we use a dataset containing paired samples $(x, t)$. Each pair is used to adjust the network parameters to minimize the difference between the network’s prediction $y$ and the actual target $t$. Thinking of the network as a function $y = f(x)$, our goal is to adjust $f(x)$ until the prediction error is as small as possible. A smaller error means the predictions closely match ground truth labels.
